content: 1. The contact person should be identified for the study, and the number of rooms available for use must be specified. 2. The condition of the rooms should be assessed to ensure they are suitable for the intended purpose. 3. It is necessary to confirm whether a toilet is available for the collection of urine samples. 4. The availability of running water in the facility should also be verified. 5. The items listed above are provided as examples, and investigators should adapt the information requirements as needed for their specific study. 6. The location or venue information is considered confidential and must be treated as such. 7. Access to these records should be restricted to a minimal number of individuals, and the records should be stored securely in locked cabinets or encrypted files. 8. Any nonessential information should be destroyed once the data collection process is complete. 9. The estimated measure of size (EMoS) is 9, and the sampling strategy is labeled as Strategy B. 10. Survey implementation and quality assurance are categorized under Section C, while data analysis and use are categorized under Section A. 11. The first stage of sampling involves time-location sampling, which includes creating a sampling frame from the venue universe and scheduling recruitment events. 12. The sampling frame is constructed as a database, with each row representing a specific time-location cluster to be sampled. 13. Time periods should be chosen to ensure they are long or short enough to yield a sufficient but manageable number of participants. For example, patrons visiting a bar in the early evening may differ from those visiting later at night. 14. The anticipated number of eligible venue patrons or attendees can be estimated during the formative assessment or through venue observation. This estimation should be conducted with great care. 15. Variables included in the sampling frame are location or venue ID, location/venue name, time period, and EMoS. 16. In Step 2 of the sampling strategy, investigators must decide whether Equal Probability Sampling (EPS) or Probability Proportional to Size (PPS) is appropriate. 17. Regardless of the chosen approach, the selected clusters should be saved with their unique cluster IDs on a separate worksheet for fieldwork planning. 18. The original sampling frame should be maintained for reference and in case a second round of cluster selection is required. 19. Sampling information should be documented according to the outlined steps, as this information is necessary for calculating sampling probabilities and nonresponse rates. 20. Field team availability should be ascertained, and dates when field staff will not be available due to holidays, vacations, or other planned absences should be blocked off on the calendar. 21. Other dates and times when events cannot occur should also be blocked off, considering factors such as staff burnout. For instance, in some settings, field teams are given a week off after four weeks of fieldwork to return to their families. 22. Sampling events should be planned and scheduled for each selected time-location cluster. 23. The specifics of scheduling should be determined based on the local context, considering factors such as field team size, geography, and infrastructure. 24. It may be helpful to order the selected venues geographically, such as from north to south or near a main highway. 25. Data requirements for calculating sampling probabilities and response rates should be highlighted. 26. Factors influencing selection probabilities in cluster sampling, particularly time-location sampling, should be carefully considered. 27. Eligibility screening should ensure that only eligible participants are included in the sampling frame. 28. Individuals who are ineligible should not be considered when computing participation rates. 29. Survey records should be securely maintained, and any lost or incomplete records should be documented. 30. Respondent-driven sampling (RDS) is a peer-driven chain-referral sampling method first implemented in 1994 by Douglas Heckathorn. 31. RDS is a probability-based methodology useful for sampling populations that lack a sampling frame. 32. It relies on participants’ ability and willingness to identify and recruit other members of the target population into the survey. 33. RDS surveys begin with a small number of participants, called seeds, who are recruited by investigators or survey staff. 34. These seeds participate in the survey and are then asked to invite peers within their social network to participate. 35. The process continues until the desired sample size is reached. 36. RDS minimizes biases associated with chain-referral sampling by limiting the number of peers each participant can recruit, preventing individuals with larger networks from dominating the sample. 37. RDS analysis accounts for different probabilities of recruitment and uses statistical weights based on participants’ personal network size and recruitment patterns to estimate the prevalence of variables of interest. 38. RDS can only be used if the target population is socially networked and its members can recognize and recruit one another. 39. All subpopulations and subgroups within the network must be connected. If this is not the case, separate RDS surveys may be required for different subgroups. 40. RDS is often employed when members of the target population do not congregate in large numbers in public venues or when stigma and discrimination make other sampling methods difficult. 41. However, RDS is not limited to hard-to-find populations and has been used to recruit groups such as university students, migrant populations, and heterosexual men and women at high risk of HIV. 42. Functional assumptions of RDS include that respondents know one another as members of the target population, are linked by a single-component network, and that the target population is large enough to allow sampling with replacement. 43. Violations of these assumptions can compromise the feasibility and validity of an RDS survey. 44. Investigators should carefully examine these assumptions during the formative assessment before developing the RDS protocol.
